solution.concept_anchor: House contempt punishments — types and due process limits

statement_analysis.statement: The punishments a House of Parliament can impose for contempt include reprimand, admonition, suspension from the service of the House, and imprisonment.
statement_analysis.reason: These four types of punishment — reprimand, admonition, suspension, and imprisonment — are the recognised forms of sanction available to the House for contempt.

statement_analysis.statement: An imprisonment order passed by the House for contempt can be appealed to the Supreme Court under Article 32 as a matter of right.
statement_analysis.reason: No appeal as of right lies to any court against a contempt punishment order of the House — while Article 32 petitions have been filed in some cases, the constitutional position after Raja Ram Pal is that courts apply proportionality review, not a straightforward appeal mechanism.

statement_analysis.statement: Unlike judicial contempt proceedings, Parliament is not constitutionally required to follow the principles of natural justice before punishing a person for contempt of the House.
statement_analysis.reason: While parliamentary contempt proceedings are not bound by the same procedural code as judicial contempt, post-Raja Ram Pal, the House must meet at least minimal standards of procedural fairness — the position that natural justice principles have zero application is overbroad.

statement_analysis.statement: Imprisonment ordered by the House for contempt operates concurrently with, and does not automatically supersede, imprisonment ordered by a court in the same matter.
statement_analysis.reason: Parliamentary imprisonment and judicial imprisonment can be concurrent — there is no constitutional provision making one automatically supersede the other, making this a constitutionally unresolved area.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) 'Only three' tempts students who correctly identify Statement 1 as correct and Statement 4 as correct but may also believe Statement 3 is correct (that Parliament is free of natural justice obligations).
elimination_logic: Statement 2 claims a right of appeal to the Supreme Court — no such right of appeal exists as a constitutional entitlement; proportionality review under Article 32 is limited and contested. Statement 2 is incorrect.

Statement 3 claims natural justice principles have absolutely no application — post-Raja Ram Pal, minimal procedural fairness is expected. 'Not constitutionally required' is an overstatement. Statement 3 is incorrect.
Statements 1 and 4 are both accurate — the four punishments are established; concurrent imprisonment with no automatic supersession is the constitutional position.
Only two statements are correct — option (a). Wait: options go Only one / Only two / Only three / All four. Two correct = option (a). Correct option is (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is the primary trap — it sounds like a fair characterisation of parliamentary privilege immunity and echoes the broader non-justiciability principle. Students who have absorbed the general idea that Parliament is the master of its own proceedings may accept Statement 3 without realising that post-Raja Ram Pal (2007), courts have asserted that minimal procedural fairness is a threshold requirement even for parliamentary contempt punishment. The zero-natural-justice position is overbroad and was implicitly rejected in the proportionality review framework.
solution.final_explanation:
The House's contempt powers are broad but not procedurally unconstrained.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The four recognised punishments are reprimand, admonition, suspension, and imprisonment.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: There is no right of appeal to the Supreme Court against a House contempt order. Limited review under Article 32 is available but is not an appeal as of right.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Saying natural justice principles have zero application is too absolute — post-Raja Ram Pal, minimal procedural fairness is constitutionally expected before punishment.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Parliamentary and judicial imprisonment can operate concurrently; there is no automatic hierarchy between them.

Value Addition:
• The intersection of Article 21 (personal liberty) and parliamentary imprisonment without judicial trial remains one of India's most unresolved constitutional tensions.
• Reprimand and admonition are the mildest forms; imprisonment is the most severe.
• Parliamentary imprisonment terminates at session's end — it cannot continue into the next session.

solution.concept_anchor: Kihoto Hollohan — anti-defection judicial review after final order
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) attributes the Kihoto Hollohan holding to the Searchlight Case, exploiting the fact that both involved constitutional limits on legislative body powers — a classic entity-swap that works on candidates who know both cases but mix their holdings.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): The Searchlight Case (MSM Sharma, 1959) held that courts cannot question internal proceedings — not that anti-defection decisions are reviewable after final order.
Eliminate (b): Raja Ram Pal (2007) established judicial review of member expulsions for proportionality — not specifically the anti-defection review after final order.
Eliminate (d): The 2024 Constitution Bench addressed bribery for vote/speech, not anti-defection proceedings.

Confirm (c): Kihoto Hollohan (1993) is the case that established that anti-defection proceedings under the Tenth Schedule are judicially reviewable after the final order, carving out an exception to Article 122's general non-justiciability.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap in option (a) is the primary trap — it pairs the Kihoto Hollohan holding with the Searchlight Case. Students who know the Searchlight Case and Kihoto Hollohan separately but haven't drilled the specific holding-to-case mapping will be drawn to option (a), especially because the Searchlight Case is the more famous privilege case and 'courts can review this' sounds like the kind of qualified position the Searchlight Case might establish.
solution.final_explanation:
Each landmark case has a distinct and specific holding in parliamentary privilege law.

• Option (a) MSM Sharma vs. Sri Krishna Sinha paired with Kihoto Hollohan's anti-defection review holding: Incorrect. MSM Sharma established non-justiciability of internal proceedings; it said nothing about anti-defection review.
• Option (b) Raja Ram Pal (2007) paired with anti-defection proceedings being reviewable after final order: Incorrect. Raja Ram Pal addressed member expulsion, not anti-defection proceedings.
• Option (c) Kihoto Hollohan (1993) — courts can review anti-defection proceedings after final order: Correct. This is the precise holding of Kihoto Hollohan.
• Option (d) 2024 Constitution Bench — anti-defection decisions reviewed for natural justice: Incorrect. The 2024 bench addressed bribery for vote/speech, not anti-defection adjudication.

Value Addition:
• Kihoto Hollohan also struck down the provision making the Speaker's disqualification decision completely unchallengeable in courts.
• The case was decided by a 3:2 majority on the judicial review question — a narrow ruling.
• Anti-defection disqualification by the Speaker is treated differently from privilege punishment by the House — the former is subject to post-order review; the latter's reviewability is governed by Article 122.

solution.concept_anchor: State legislature privilege limits — cannot punish High Court judge; MSM Sharma press freedom

statement_analysis.statement: A state legislature can initiate contempt proceedings and impose punishment on a sitting High Court judge for remarks made in a judgment that the legislature considers to be an affront to its dignity.
statement_analysis.reason: State legislature privileges do not extend to punishing a High Court judge for judicial pronouncements — judges acting in their judicial capacity are protected, and the legislature's privilege cannot override the constitutional independence of the judiciary.

statement_analysis.statement: The Searchlight Case established that state legislature privileges under Article 194 are not subordinate to the press freedom guaranteed by Article 19(1)(a) when the legislature determines that a report is inaccurate.
statement_analysis.reason: The Searchlight Case established precisely the opposite — state legislature privileges cannot be used to penalise the press for publishing a substantially true report; press freedom under Article 19(1)(a) limits the reach of Article 194 privileges in such cases.

statement_analysis.statement: While Article 194 mirrors Article 105 structurally, state legislatures in practice have sometimes claimed privileges broader than what the constitutional text or judicial precedent supports.
statement_analysis.reason: This is a historically documented pattern — state legislatures have on multiple occasions claimed privilege powers that went beyond their constitutional entitlement, leading to judicial intervention in several cases including the Searchlight Case itself.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) would suggest Statements 2 and 3 are incorrect; students who correctly identify Statement 2 as reversing the Searchlight holding might also mistakenly believe Statement 3 is also incorrect because it seems like a criticism of state legislatures, not a factual claim.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 claims state legislatures can punish High Court judges — this exceeds their privilege powers; judicial independence bars such action. Statement 1 is incorrect.
Statement 2 reverses the Searchlight Case holding — the case protected press freedom against state legislature privilege, not the reverse. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 3 accurately describes the historical pattern of state legislatures overclaiming privilege powers. Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 2 are incorrect — option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2's reversal of the Searchlight Case holding is the central trap. The case is well known, but its direction — who prevailed — is frequently confused. Students who associate 'Searchlight Case = privilege vs. press' without remembering that the press prevailed (privilege was limited) will accept Statement 2 as true, making it a clean reversed-causation variant within a multi-statement format.
solution.final_explanation:
State legislature privileges under Article 194 have real constitutional limits that the Searchlight Case and subsequent decisions have defined.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Privileges cannot be used to punish a High Court judge for judicial pronouncements. Judicial independence under Articles 121 and 211 (and analogous principles) bars such action.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The Searchlight Case held that state legislature privileges are LIMITED by press freedom — the press, when publishing a substantially true report, cannot be penalised through privilege proceedings. The statement reverses the actual holding.
• Statement 3 — Correct: State legislatures have historically overclaimed their privilege powers — the Searchlight Case itself arose from Bihar Assembly exceeding its privilege entitlement.

Value Addition:
• Article 211 bars state legislatures from discussing the conduct of High Court judges in their judicial capacity — complementing the judicial independence argument.
• The MSM Sharma principle has been applied symmetrically to Parliament and state legislatures.
• Overclaiming privilege remains a live issue — courts have repeatedly had to define the outer limits of legislative privilege at both the central and state level.

solution.concept_anchor: Sting footage inside House — whether 'proceeding in Parliament'; social media by MPs

statement_analysis.statement: Sting operation footage screened on the floor of the House of Parliament during its proceedings constitutes a 'proceeding in Parliament' within the meaning of Article 105, attracting the full protection of parliamentary privilege.
statement_analysis.reason: When sting footage is formally introduced and shown during a sitting of the House, it becomes part of the proceedings of Parliament — the constitutional protection of proceedings under Article 105 applies to what happens within the House's formal sittings, regardless of the evidentiary form.

statement_analysis.statement: An MP who reproduces or reposts on a personal social media account the verbatim contents of a parliamentary speech they delivered in the House is covered by the parliamentary privilege under Article 105(2), because the content originated in the protected space of Parliament.
statement_analysis.reason: Parliamentary privilege protects what is said and done within the House — it does not automatically travel with the member outside the House. Social media reproduction of parliamentary speech outside Parliament does not attract Article 105(2) protection; it is subject to ordinary law including defamation.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Wait, correct option is (a). The strong distractor is option (c), which says Statement 1 is correct but Statement 2 is incorrect — identical to the correct answer. Let me re-evaluate: correct option (a) means both statements are correct, but Statement 2 is incorrect. Rechecking — option (a) in this format is 'Both correct', option (b) is 'Both incorrect', option (c) is 'Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect', option (d) is 'Statement 1 incorrect, Statement 2 correct.' Statement 1 is correct; Statement 2 is incorrect. Correct option is (c).
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Sting footage formally shown on the floor during proceedings becomes part of those proceedings — Article 105 protection applies. Statement 1 is correct.

Statement 2: Social media reproduction of parliamentary speech outside the House is not covered by Article 105(2) — the privilege is location-and-process bound, not content-bound. The protection does not follow the member's words outside Parliament. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct + Statement 2 incorrect — option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the intuitive but legally incorrect assumption that a member 'owns' their parliamentary privilege with respect to their own words — so that whatever they said in Parliament, they can freely reproduce anywhere. The privilege attaches to the act of speaking within the House, not to the words themselves as portable content. A student who conflates 'I said this in Parliament, so I can repeat it anywhere with impunity' will mark Statement 2 as correct and choose option (a).
solution.final_explanation:
Parliamentary privilege is process-bound and location-sensitive.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Sting footage formally introduced and screened during a sitting of the House becomes part of the proceedings — Article 105 protection attaches to all formal acts within the House's sittings.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Social media posts by an MP reproducing their own parliamentary speech are outside the House and outside the privilege shield. Article 105(2) protects what is said and done in Parliament — not its external re-publication by the member. An MP who tweets their parliamentary speech and it contains defamatory content can face legal proceedings for the tweet.

Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — option (c).

Value Addition:
• This distinction (in-House = protected; out-of-House reproduction = unprotected) is the basis on which defamation cases against MPs for out-of-Parliament statements are maintainable.
• Live broadcasts of parliamentary proceedings are authorised by the Houses — broadcasters enjoy a derived protection for technical errors in transmission of authorised content.
• The cash-for-query sting footage (2005) was screened in the House, contributing to its status as a parliamentary proceeding for subsequent judicial review purposes.

solution.concept_anchor: Privilege procedure — matching stages to correct actors/outcomes
solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) correctly places the Privilege Committee's recommendatory role (C-2) but assigns the final punishment authority to the Speaker rather than the full House (D-4 vs D-3), trapping students who know the committee is recommendatory but misconstrue who makes the final decision.
elimination_logic: A (member's written notice) — the first step in privilege proceedings is a member giving written notice to the Speaker/Chairman; matches with 3 (Speaker/Chairman's consent as first filter).

B (Privilege Committee's report) — the committee investigates and produces a recommendatory report; this goes to the full House, not to the Speaker alone; matches with 4 (full House votes on committee's report).
C (Full House vote on punishment) — the House decides the final punishment; matches with 1 (final authority for punishment rests with full House).
D (Speaker's role at admission stage) — the Speaker's consent is discretionary and is the first filter; matches with 2. Correct combination: A-3, B-4, C-1, D-2 — option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap between options (b) and (d) targets the confusion about whether the Speaker or the full House makes the final punishment decision. Many students know the Speaker has a central role in privilege matters and may place the final authority with the Speaker rather than the House. The Privilege Committee's recommendatory nature is widely known, but the precise flow — committee report → House vote → House decides punishment — is confused when the Speaker's prominent role is over-weighted.
solution.final_explanation:
Privilege proceedings in Parliament follow a structured procedural flow:

• A — Member gives written notice: This is the initiation step — matched with the Speaker/Chairman's consent as the first filter (3).
• B — Privilege Committee's report: After investigation, the committee produces a recommendation — this goes to the full House for decision (4).
• C — Full House vote: The House, not the committee or the Speaker, has the final authority to impose punishment (1).
• D — Speaker's discretion at admission: The Speaker's consent at the notice stage is discretionary and filters what reaches the committee (2).

Correct matching: A-3, B-4, C-1, D-2 — option (b).

Value Addition:
• The Speaker can also suo motu refer privilege matters — the member's notice is one initiation route, not the only one.
• Lok Sabha Privilege Committee has 15 members; Rajya Sabha has 10.
• The committee's findings are only recommendatory — the House is both the judge and the punisher, a feature distinguishing parliamentary contempt from judicial contempt.

solution.concept_anchor: RTI vs. parliamentary privilege — Section 8 exemptions and Speaker's non-disclosure position
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) suggests the Speaker's position must give way entirely to RTI because Parliament is a public authority — this tempts students who recall that Parliament is covered by the RTI Act without knowing the Section 8 exemptions and privilege protection.
elimination_logic: Parliament is a public authority under the RTI Act — this is established. But being a public authority does not make all records freely accessible.
Section 8 exemptions cover deliberative processes; parliamentary privilege provides an additional protection layer for committee deliberations.

Eliminate (a): Being a public authority does not override Section 8 exemptions or parliamentary privilege over committee deliberations — the Speaker's position is constitutionally grounded, not arbitrary.

Eliminate (b): The CIC's RTI jurisdiction does not automatically override parliamentary privilege for internal deliberative records — the two operate in different constitutional spaces. Confirm (c): The correct position is that Parliament is subject to RTI but Section 8 exemptions and parliamentary privilege jointly limit what must be disclosed from committee deliberations — the CIC-vs-Speaker tension remains unresolved by any Supreme Court ruling.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is the public-authority-equals-full-disclosure leap. Students who recall that Parliament is a public authority under the RTI Act may conclude that the Speaker's non-disclosure position is legally unsustainable. The nuance — that public authority status coexists with Section 8 exemptions and parliamentary privilege as limiting principles — is the precise constitutional complexity this question tests.
solution.final_explanation:
The RTI Act creates a disclosure obligation for Parliament as a public authority, but not an absolute one.

In the scenario, the key question is whether the Speaker can legitimately withhold committee deliberations from RTI disclosure.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Parliament being a public authority does not automatically negate the Speaker's position. Section 8 exemptions and parliamentary privilege jointly limit the scope of mandatory disclosure.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The CIC's jurisdiction over parliamentary records does not override parliamentary privilege — the constitutional space occupied by Article 105 is not dissolved by RTI jurisdiction.
• Option (c) — Correct: This accurately captures the layered position — Parliament is subject to RTI, but Section 8 exemptions (covering deliberative processes) and parliamentary privilege over committee deliberations create legitimate grounds for non-disclosure. The CIC-vs-Speaker tension is a live, unresolved constitutional question.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Article 122 protects parliamentary proceedings from judicial inquiry into procedural irregularities — it is not directly the basis for RTI exemption from the CIC's jurisdiction; the RTI exemption argument is better grounded in Section 8 and parliamentary privilege.

Value Addition:
• Section 8(1)(i) RTI Act exempts Cabinet papers and similar deliberations — parliamentary committee deliberations can be analogously claimed.
• No Supreme Court ruling has definitively adjudicated the CIC-vs-Speaker boundary on parliamentary records.
• The Speaker's Secretariat is a distinct entity from Parliament itself — its records may have a different RTI exposure profile.

solution.concept_anchor: Key privilege-related constitutional and legislative events in sequence
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) places the Kihoto Hollohan case before the Raja Ram Pal case, which is correct on the case dates (1993 before 2007), but also places the 2024 bench ruling as occurring before the RTI Act, which is obviously wrong — the partial correctness of the first swap distracts students from examining the second.
elimination_logic: Kihoto Hollohan (1993) preceded Raja Ram Pal (2007) — the 1993 date is the earlier case; anti-defection review before member expulsion review.
RTI Act (2005) falls between the two cases — after Kihoto Hollohan (1993) but before Raja Ram Pal (2007).
2024 Constitution Bench on bribery and privilege is the most recent event — must be last.
Correct order: Kihoto Hollohan (1993) → RTI Act (2005) → Raja Ram Pal (2007) → 2024 Constitution Bench — option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The RTI Act (2005) is the inserted event that tests whether students know it falls between the two major privilege cases. Option (b) places the RTI Act correctly in relation to Raja Ram Pal but swaps the 2024 bench's position, creating a partially plausible wrong sequence. Students who focus on the case-to-case ordering and don't track the RTI Act's year precisely will choose option (b).
solution.final_explanation:
The chronological sequence of landmark privilege-related milestones:

1. Kihoto Hollohan vs. Zachillhu (1993): Supreme Court rules anti-defection proceedings are judicially reviewable after final order.
2. RTI Act (2005): Parliament designated a public authority — creating the privilege-vs-disclosure tension.
3. Raja Ram Pal vs. Speaker, Lok Sabha (2007): Supreme Court upholds judicial review of member expulsion on proportionality grounds.
4. Seven-Judge Constitution Bench (2024): Unanimously overrules 1998 JMM Bribery Case ruling — bribery for vote/speech not protected.

Correct order: 1993 → 2005 → 2007 → 2024 — option (d).

Value Addition:
• Each of these milestones progressively narrowed the scope of absolute parliamentary privilege immunity.
• The cash-for-query scandal (2005) and the resulting Raja Ram Pal case directly followed the RTI Act's enactment — both are 2005–2007 developments.
• The 2024 ruling is the most recent and most significant contraction of parliamentary privilege — a mandatory exam update.

solution.concept_anchor: Post-44th Amendment vacuum — privileges undefined; basic structure limits apply

statement_analysis.statement: After the 44th Constitutional Amendment, 1978, parliamentary privileges in India exist in a definitional vacuum — they are neither enumerated in the Constitution nor governed by a separate Parliamentary Privileges Act.
statement_analysis.reason: The 44th Amendment removed the House of Commons benchmark but did not replace it with any codified list or legislative enactment — the resulting vacuum means privilege content is derived from practice and judicial pronouncements rather than text.

statement_analysis.statement: The absence of codification of parliamentary privileges is constitutionally irrelevant because Articles 105 and 194 themselves, by incorporating an open-ended framework, provide sufficient legal certainty.
statement_analysis.reason: The absence of codification is constitutionally significant — it creates uncertainty about privilege scope, enables overclaiming, and has been criticised by the First Press Commission and other bodies; 'sufficient legal certainty' is an overstatement not supported by the judicial record.

statement_analysis.statement: Even if Parliament were to enact a law codifying its privileges, such a law would be subject to the basic structure doctrine — it cannot codify a privilege in a manner that destroys the basic structure of the Constitution.
statement_analysis.reason: Post-Kesavananda Bharati, no constitutional or statutory provision can override the basic structure — a codification Act would be subject to this limit.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) would require all three statements to be correct; students who accept the 'open-ended framework = sufficient certainty' reasoning in Statement 2 without examining it critically will choose (d).
elimination_logic: Statement 2 claims the open-ended framework provides 'sufficient legal certainty' — this contradicts decades of criticism, judicial uncertainty, and calls for codification. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correctly describes the post-44th Amendment vacuum. Statement 1 is correct.
Statement 3 correctly applies the basic structure doctrine to any future codification attempt. Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 are correct — option (a).
solution.final_explanation:
The post-44th Amendment privilege landscape is one of deliberate constitutional incompleteness.

• Statement 1 — Correct: No enumeration, no Privileges Act — the definitional vacuum is a documented constitutional reality post-1978.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: 'Sufficient legal certainty' is factually wrong. The open-ended framework has generated significant uncertainty, litigation, and criticism. Multiple bodies have recommended codification precisely because of this uncertainty.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Kesavananda Bharati's basic structure doctrine constrains even parliamentary legislation — any future Privileges Act would be subject to this limit.

Value Addition:
• India is among the few Westminster-model democracies that have not enacted a dedicated parliamentary privileges statute.
• The UK's Parliamentary Standards Act provides a comparative benchmark for what codification can look like.
• The basic structure doctrine has never been directly applied to a privilege claim, but its applicability to all constitutional powers is well-established.

solution.concept_anchor: Expulsion vs. suspension — who orders, duration, finality
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) claims both expulsion and suspension are ordered by the Speaker/Chairman, which conflates the two powers — a student who knows the Speaker/Chairman is central to privilege matters may assign both to the presiding officer without distinguishing expulsion (full House) from suspension (Speaker/House).
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Expulsion is not temporary — it is permanent (until re-election or further House decision). Suspension is temporary.
Eliminate (b): Expulsion is ordered by the full House, not by the Speaker/Chairman alone — conflating the two is incorrect.
Eliminate (d): An expelled member does NOT lose the right to contest a by-election — there is no constitutional bar preventing an expelled member from immediately contesting re-election.
Confirm (c): Expulsion is a permanent removal by the full House; suspension is temporary and can be ordered by the Speaker/Chairman or by the House — option (c) correctly draws this distinction.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (b) is the entity-swap trap — assigning the expulsion power to the Speaker/Chairman rather than the full House. Students who know the Speaker/Chairman is the dominant figure in privilege proceedings often conflate the admission-stage gatekeeping function with the final expulsion power. The distinction — Speaker/Chairman for suspension; full House for expulsion — is precise and examinable.
solution.final_explanation:
Expulsion and suspension are the two major disciplinary actions against members, but they differ fundamentally in who orders them and their duration.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Expulsion is not temporary; it is permanent removal from the House.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Expulsion is ordered by the full House; suspension can be ordered by the Speaker/Chairman or the House. The two powers are not both exercisable by the Speaker/Chairman.
• Option (c) — Correct: Expulsion = permanent, by full House; suspension = temporary, by Speaker/Chairman or House. This is the correct distinction.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: An expelled member retains the constitutional right to contest a by-election — no re-election bar is imposed by expulsion.

Value Addition:
• The Raja Ram Pal case (2007) confirmed that expulsion is judicially reviewable for proportionality — making it less than absolutely final.
• A member suspended by the House loses rights and privileges for the duration of suspension but is not removed from membership.
• In the 2005 cash-for-query episode, expelled members could immediately seek re-election from their constituencies.
